newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Talk of Brazil trade surplus raises eyebrows.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Talk of Brazil trade surplus raises eyebrows.

text.p: Brazil may officially post its first trade surplus in seven months in January, but economists say the figure would have probably been in the red had it not been for problems with a new computerized import registry.

Many goods destined to enter Brazil in January were still waiting to be liberated by customs officials who were bogged down with problems in the Siscomex registry, which began tracking imports on Jan 1, economists said.
"We won't really know what January's true imports were until we get combined figures for February," said Dany Rappaport, chief economist for MCM Consultores in Brazil.
MCM had forecast a $1.0 billion trade deficit for January, in line with a Reuter survey of eight banks and research firms that put January's trade gap at $900 million.
But government documents obtained by Reuters on Friday showed that Brazil's trade accounts posted a $220 million trade surplus through Jan 28.
In addition, a commerce ministry official said Brazil would close January with its trade accounts in balance and that Siscomex in no way slowed the level of imports.

"The result is absolutely real. Any problems in the first week of the functioning of the Siscomex system were fully absorbed in following weeks," Mauricio Cortes, secretary of foreign trade at the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters in an interview.

Cortes said importers, hoping to avoid anticipated start-up problems with Siscomex, brought in January orders in December, which pushed December's gap to a monthly record of $1.79 billion and slowed imports in January.

Although economists acknowledged that fears over Siscomex undoubtedly pushed up December imports and thereby cut into January's, they said it would have been nearly impossible for Brazil to have posted a "real" trade surplus this month.
"This surplus is a distortion that has to be adjusted in February to arrive at an accurate monthly average," said Marcelo Audi, head of research for Merrill Lynch in Brazil.

"Independent of Siscomex, a trade surplus would have been impossible in January. Imports were definitely lower in January for seasonal reasons but so were exports," said an economist at a leading international bank who requested anonymity.
One economist, however, said he saw something positive in today's figures.
"I was expecting a sizeable deficit even with Siscomex problems, so if they do post a surplus it is a good sign," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC bank in Brazil.
Brazil is not expected to register an actual trade surplus until April, when the nation's agricultural crops begin being harvested. The nation has not seen a monthly trade surplus since May 1996.
Brazil posted a record $5.5 billion trade gap in 1996, following a $3.52 billion shortfall in 1995.
